title: The users schema
idea: A Drizzle schema describes a table in JavaScript. Each key becomes a column, with a type and rules such as `notNull` and `unique`.
points: `pgTable('users', { ... })` names the table and declares its columns.
Rows come back with the JavaScript keys, so your code reads `passwordHash`.
`notNull()` and `unique()` are rules the database enforces, even if your code forgets.
`npx drizzle-kit push` creates the table from this file; queries then import `users`.

hero.caption: Two keys differ from their columns: JavaScript uses camelCase, SQL uses snake_case.

code.title: The users table
code.caption: Save the schema block as `src/db/schema.js`. Everything below it is setup, so this file runs alone.

walk.text: The table `users`. A `serial` primary key: Postgres supplies each `id`.
`notNull().unique()`: Postgres refuses a missing or repeated email.
The key `passwordHash` maps to the column `password_hash`.
`defaultNow()`: Postgres fills `created_at` when a row is inserted.
`drizzle-kit push` is not run here, so raw SQL creates the same table.
Insert without `id` or `createdAt`. The row comes back with camelCase keys and both filled in.
Break each rule. `err.cause.code` is the Postgres code: `23505` unique, `23502` not null.

pitfalls: Editing `schema.js` does not change an existing table. Run `drizzle-kit push` again.
Do not check for a duplicate email in JavaScript first. Two requests can pass at once.
Never store a plain password in `passwordHash`. Store the bcrypt hash.

quiz.why: `select()` returns every column under the keys declared in the schema. The snake_case names stay inside SQL.

takeaway: The schema is the table's contract; the database enforces its rules.
